pathway.title: Software Development
pathway.description: Learn a disciplined path from software needs and requirements through design, implementation, verification, release, and maintenance.

course.title: Software Development — Beginner
course.short_description: A complete introduction to software development practice: requirements, design, version control, review, testing, debugging, security, accessibility, release, and maintenance.
course.prerequisites: No professional software-development experience required. Learners should be able to read simple Python code and use a school-approved development environment.
learning_outcomes: Describe a software lifecycle and turn needs into testable requirements.
Decompose work into slices and design focused modules with clear interfaces.
Use version-control, review, testing, debugging, and documentation practices.
Build security, accessibility, privacy, and maintainability into development work.
Plan, release, and maintain a small software product honestly and safely.
course.dependencies: Python 3.10+ standard library only; no third-party packages required.

modules.title: Discover and define the work
modules.description: Understand lifecycles, requirements, acceptance criteria, and useful slices.

topics.title: Understand the software development lifecycle
topics.description: A lifecycle gives a team a repeatable path from a problem to a maintained product.

lesson.title: Understand the software development lifecycle
objectives: Name the major lifecycle stages.
Explain why feedback can move work backward.
Match a useful artifact to each stage.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A lifecycle gives a team a repeatable path from a problem to a maintained product. Common stages include discovery, requirements, design, implementation, verification, release, and maintenance; real teams may loop between them rather than follow a one-way staircase. The lifecycle is useful because it makes work and decisions visible, not because every project must use identical documents. A small change still benefits from asking who needs it, what success means, how it will be tested, and how it will be supported after release. Software development is a disciplined way to turn a need into a useful, supportable product. A developer should make the problem visible before choosing code, because unclear assumptions become expensive defects later. Use small artifacts such as a requirement, diagram, test, commit, or decision note to create shared understanding with other people. Keep responsibilities separate, name constraints, and prefer a simple design that can be inspected and changed. Examples in this course use Python 3.10+ standard-library code so the software behavior can be demonstrated without a network, account, or third-party package. The same habits apply to other languages and teams: clarify expected behavior, implement a small slice, verify it, review the result, and record what remains limited. A professional solution also considers accessibility, privacy, security, maintainability, and how a future developer will operate and improve the system.

topics.title: Write requirements, user stories, and acceptance criteria
topics.description: A requirement describes a need or constraint that software should satisfy.

lesson.title: Write requirements, user stories, and acceptance criteria
objectives: Distinguish a need from an implementation detail.
Write testable acceptance criteria.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A requirement describes a need or constraint that software should satisfy. A user story is a concise perspective such as “As a reader, I want to find a title so that I can choose a book.” Acceptance criteria turn an idea into observable conditions. Good criteria are specific enough to test, avoid prescribing unnecessary implementation, and include important failure or boundary behavior. Separate functional requirements from quality attributes such as accessibility, performance, privacy, and security. Ask questions when a statement has hidden assumptions, undefined words, or conflicting priorities. Software development is a disciplined way to turn a need into a useful, supportable product. A developer should make the problem visible before choosing code, because unclear assumptions become expensive defects later. Use small artifacts such as a requirement, diagram, test, commit, or decision note to create shared understanding with other people. Keep responsibilities separate, name constraints, and prefer a simple design that can be inspected and changed. Examples in this course use Python 3.10+ standard-library code so the software behavior can be demonstrated without a network, account, or third-party package. The same habits apply to other languages and teams: clarify expected behavior, implement a small slice, verify it, review the result, and record what remains limited. A professional solution also considers accessibility, privacy, security, maintainability, and how a future developer will operate and improve the system.

blocks.title: Understand the idea

lesson.title: Design modules, interfaces, and responsibilities
objectives: Describe cohesion and coupling.
Define a small interface.
Explain how dependency injection improves testing or change.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A module should have a focused responsibility and a small interface. An interface describes what a component offers without forcing callers to know how it works. Cohesion asks whether related things belong together; coupling asks how much one component depends on another. Dependency injection can supply a collaborator such as a clock or repository, making the core behavior easier to test. Design is a set of trade-offs: split components when boundaries clarify change, not merely to create more files. Software development is a disciplined way to turn a need into a useful, supportable product. Use small artifacts such as a requirement, diagram, test, commit, or decision note to create shared understanding with other people. Keep responsibilities separate, name constraints, and prefer a simple design that can be inspected and changed. Examples in this course use Python 3.10+ standard-library code so the software behavior can be demonstrated without a network, account, or third-party package. The same habits apply to other languages and teams: clarify expected behavior, implement a small slice, verify it, review the result, and record what remains limited. A professional solution also considers accessibility, privacy, security, maintainability, and how a future developer will operate and improve the system.

lesson.title: Use version control concepts and meaningful commits
objectives: Explain commit, branch, and review concepts.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Version control records changes so a team can understand, compare, review, and recover work. A commit should represent a coherent change with a useful message, not a random save point. A branch isolates work while the main line remains understandable. Pull requests or equivalent reviews provide discussion and automated checks before integration. Never commit secrets, generated dependencies, or unrelated personal files. Version control is not a substitute for backups, tests, or communication; it is a tool that supports them. blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A code review checks behavior, design, readability, tests, security, and maintainability. lesson.title: Debug with hypotheses, logs, and minimal reproductions
objectives: Reduce a failure to a minimal reproduction.
Use evidence and a hypothesis rather than random edits.
Add a regression test after a fix.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Debugging is a structured investigation. Reproduce the failure, read the traceback or evidence, reduce the input, state a hypothesis, and change one thing at a time. Logging can reveal state transitions without changing the result, but logs should not expose secrets or unnecessary personal information. Once fixed, add a regression test that would have failed before the fix. Avoid random edits and broad exception handling that hides the cause. blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Security, accessibility, and privacy are development requirements, not polish added at the end. Validate untrusted input, use least privilege, avoid secrets in source, and design errors that do not reveal sensitive internals. Accessibility includes keyboard operation, readable labels, sufficient contrast, clear focus, and understandable messages. Privacy means collecting only what is needed, explaining use, limiting retention, and protecting access. Threat modelling asks what could go wrong, who could be affected, and which control reduces the risk. A small offline program still benefits from these habits. topics.title: Maintain, refactor, and manage technical debt
topics.description: Maintenance includes fixing defects, adapting to new requirements, improving operations, and removing obsolete code.

lesson.title: Maintain, refactor, and manage technical debt
objectives: Distinguish refactoring from behavior change.
Describe and prioritize technical debt.
Use tests and a baseline to make maintenance safe.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Maintenance includes fixing defects, adapting to new requirements, improving operations, and removing obsolete code. Refactoring changes internal structure while preserving externally tested behavior. Technical debt is a trade-off that creates future cost; it is manageable when recorded, bounded, and repaid deliberately. Before refactoring, establish tests and a baseline. Make one coherent change, run checks, and review the diff. Avoid using “clean-up” as permission for unrelated scope. A maintainable system makes the next change safer, not merely the current code prettier. Software development is a disciplined way to turn a need into a useful, supportable product. A developer should make the problem visible before choosing code, because unclear assumptions become expensive defects later. Use small artifacts such as a requirement, diagram, test, commit, or decision note to create shared understanding with other people. Keep responsibilities separate, name constraints, and prefer a simple design that can be inspected and changed. Examples in this course use Python 3.10+ standard-library code so the software behavior can be demonstrated without a network, account, or third-party package. The same habits apply to other languages and teams: clarify expected behavior, implement a small slice, verify it, review the result, and record what remains limited. A professional solution also considers accessibility, privacy, security, maintainability, and how a future developer will operate and improve the system.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The example shows one small, observable slice of the development idea. Read the requirement, trace the implementation, compare the output with the acceptance condition, and identify one change that would require a new test or documentation update.

blocks.title: Offline Task List: From Requirement to Release
blocks.purpose: Develop a small offline task-list application while demonstrating the complete software-development process: requirements, design, version-control evidence, testing, secure and inclusive behavior, release documentation, and maintenance planning.
privacy_and_limits: Use fictional task text only; do not collect names, contact details, passwords, or learner identifiers.
Keep the application offline and in memory or a controlled local file; do not claim that deployment, backups, or multi-user security were verified.
Use Python 3.10+ standard library only and document limitations clearly.
requirements: Write a user story and at least six acceptance criteria, including normal, empty, invalid, accessibility, and privacy behavior.
Separate input, task-domain, and storage responsibilities with a small documented interface.
Support adding, listing, searching, completing, and safely rejecting blank or duplicate tasks.
Use meaningful version-control-style commits or a commit plan for the feature slices.
Add deterministic unit checks and at least one integration-style check across components.
Handle errors without crashing or revealing sensitive implementation details.
Provide a README, release checklist, risk table, and one maintenance or technical-debt note.
suggested_steps: Write the story, acceptance criteria, risk table, and slice plan.
Design interfaces and implement the smallest vertical slice.
Add validation, tests, and an integration check.
Review security, accessibility, privacy, documentation, and release evidence.
Record a maintenance improvement and explain what remains unverified.
success_checks: Every required operation has observable acceptance evidence.
Blank, duplicate, empty, missing, and repeated cases are handled safely.
Tests are repeatable and include both component and collaboration behavior.
The README and release checklist let another developer reproduce local verification.
Security, accessibility, privacy, limitations, and technical debt are explicitly documented.

rubric.look_for: Clear story, acceptance criteria, slices, dependencies, risks, and definition of done.
Focused responsibilities, interfaces, correct operations, and maintainable Python code.
Deterministic unit/integration evidence, edge cases, minimal reproduction, and regression test.
Safe validation, inclusive criteria, data minimization, and honest limitations.
Commit/review evidence, README, release checklist, and technical-debt plan.
